expectations.text: Does NOT simply say scalar invariance failed so group mean comparison is impossible
expectations.evidence: Response opens with 'Yes, you can still compare latent means' and explains the partial invariance fallback, never claiming comparison is impossible.

expectations.text: Explains partial scalar invariance as a legitimate fallback when only a subset of items fail scalar constraints
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly names Byrne, Shavelson & Muthén (1989) and describes partial scalar invariance as 'a defensible fallback when only a subset of items drive the failure.'

expectations.text: States or implies a threshold for acceptable partial invariance — releasing ~20% of intercepts (here 2 of 9 = 22%) is at the edge; 1-2 items is more defensible
expectations.evidence: Condition 1 explicitly states the ~20% rule, calculates 2/9 = 22%, calls it 'right at the edge,' notes one item would be 'clearly defensible' while two is 'borderline,' and instructs the user to 'acknowledge that explicitly when you report this.'

expectations.text: Explains that the non-invariant items must be freed AND that at least 2 intercepts per factor must remain constrained for identification
expectations.evidence: Condition 2 names the identification requirement (citing Steenkamp & Baumgartner, 1998), states 'each factor needs at least two intercepts that remain fixed,' and flags the concrete failure case where two non-invariant items on a 3-item factor would leave only one anchor.

expectations.text: Requires substantive justification for why those specific items have different intercepts across groups — not just MI-based releasing
expectations.evidence: Condition 3 calls this 'the most important condition and the one most often skipped,' explicitly labels MI-only releasing as 'exploratory post-hoc fitting,' and provides concrete examples of the kind of theoretical account needed (somatic endorsement norms, cultural referents, diagnostic criterion overlap).

expectations.text: States that mean comparison with partial scalar invariance is defensible if conditions are met, but should be explicitly reported as partial rather than full invariance
expectations.evidence: The reporting section states 'Don't present this as full scalar invariance' and specifies exactly what to disclose, ending with 'The mean comparison is defensible — but the caveats are load-bearing, not boilerplate.'
